meta.title: The balance sheet, cash flows and disclosure
meta.summary: Usefulness and limits of the balance sheet, classification of assets, liabilities and equity, liquidity and solvency ratios, the purpose and sections of the statement of cash flows, free cash flow, and disclosure techniques.

videos.title: What the balance sheet tells you
videos.take: The balance sheet shows liquidity, solvency and financial flexibility, but omits much of a company's value

scenes.say: Bluestem's bank reads the balance sheet first. It wants to know: can this company pay us back?

scenes.heading: What it helps assess
items: Solvency: paying debts as they mature
scenes.say: The balance sheet helps assess liquidity, how soon assets turn into cash; solvency, the ability to pay debts as they come due; and financial flexibility, the ability to raise cash and adapt to surprises.

scenes.heading: Limitations
scenes.say: But it has limits. Most assets are at historical cost, not current value. Many amounts are estimates. And some of the most valuable things, like Bluestem's brand and its designers' know-how, don't appear at all.

sub: than equity on the balance sheet
scenes.say: That's why companies often sell for much more than their book equity. When Bluestem goes public, its market value will likely be several times its book value.
And remember, it's a snapshot at one date. The income statement and cash flow statement cover a period.

scenes.q: The ability to pay debts as they mature over the long term is:
scenes.say: Quick check. The ability to pay debts as they mature over the long term is called what? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Classifying assets
videos.take: Current assets will be used or turned into cash within a year or the operating cycle, whichever is longer

scenes.say: A classified balance sheet groups similar items so users can see liquidity at a glance.

sub: Expected to be converted to cash, sold or used
within one year or the operating cycle
scenes.say: Current assets are cash and other assets expected to be converted to cash, sold or consumed within one year or the operating cycle, whichever is longer. They're listed in order of liquidity.

scenes.heading: Current assets
scenes.say: Typical current assets: cash and cash equivalents; short-term investments; receivables, net of the allowance for doubtful accounts; inventories; and prepaid expenses.

scenes.heading: Noncurrent assets
scenes.say: Noncurrent assets include long-term investments, like bonds held to maturity or land held for a future plant; property, plant and equipment, net of accumulated depreciation; intangible assets; and other assets.

sub: Cash set aside to repay long-term
scenes.say: Watch out: cash restricted for a long-term purpose, like a sinking fund to repay bonds in five years, isn't a current asset. Classification follows the expected use.

scenes.q: Land held for a future plant site is classified as:
scenes.say: Quick check. Land held for a future plant site is classified as what? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, a long-term investment. It isn't used in operations yet.

videos.title: Classifying liabilities and equity
videos.take: Current liabilities are paid from current assets within a year; equity shows contributed capital, retained earnings and AOCI

scenes.say: The right side of the balance sheet: who has claims on the assets?

scenes.heading: Current liabilities
scenes.say: Current liabilities are obligations expected to be paid from current assets, or by creating other current liabilities, within a year or the operating cycle: accounts payable, accrued liabilities, unearned revenue, and the current portion of long-term debt.

sub: $100,000 of the term loan due next year
scenes.say: Bluestem's term loan is repaid $100,000 a year. Next year's $100,000 is reported as current; the rest stays long-term.

scenes.heading: Stockholders' equity
scenes.say: Stockholders' equity includes capital stock at par value; additional paid-in capital above par; retained earnings; accumulated other comprehensive income; less treasury stock the company has bought back. Noncontrolling interests in subsidiaries also appear within equity.
Some instruments, like mandatorily redeemable preferred stock, look like equity but are liabilities. You'll sort those out in Intermediate Accounting Two.

scenes.q: A 5-year note has $40,000 due next year. On the balance sheet, $40,000 is:
scenes.say: Quick check. A five-year note has forty thousand dollars due next year. How is that forty thousand reported? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Bluestem's balance sheet and ratios
videos.take: Current ratio and debt to assets turn the balance sheet into liquidity and solvency measures

scenes.say: Here's Bluestem's balance sheet at December 31, 2027, condensed.

scenes.heading: Assets
scenes.say: Current assets total $1.4 million: cash, receivables, inventories and prepaids. Long-term investments, property and intangibles add $2.6 million. Total assets: $4 million.

scenes.heading: Liabilities and equity
scenes.say: Current liabilities are $650,000 and long-term debt $900,000: total liabilities $1.55 million. Equity is common stock and paid-in capital of $367,500, retained earnings of $2,062,500, and accumulated OCI of $20,000. It balances at $4 million.

scenes.heading: Two key ratios
scenes.say: The current ratio is current assets over current liabilities: two point one five, comfortable. Debt to assets is total liabilities over total assets: thirty-eight point eight percent.
But more than half of current assets is inventory. The quick ratio, cash plus receivables over current liabilities, is only point nine two. Kayaks aren't cash until they're sold.

scenes.q: Current assets $900,000; current liabilities $600,000. Current ratio?
scenes.say: Quick check. Current assets nine hundred thousand; current liabilities six hundred thousand. Current ratio? Pause and pick.

videos.title: The statement of cash flows: an overview
videos.take: Cash flows are classified as operating, investing or financing; free cash flow shows discretionary cash

scenes.say: Profit isn't cash. The statement of cash flows shows where Bluestem's cash actually came from and went.

scenes.heading: Three activities
scenes.say: Operating activities are the cash effects of earning income: collections from customers and payments to suppliers, employees and the government. Investing covers buying and selling long-term assets and investments. Financing covers borrowing, repaying, issuing stock and paying dividends.

scenes.heading: Bluestem, 2027
scenes.say: Bluestem generated $520,000 from operations, used $410,000 in investing, mostly new molds, and $60,000 in financing: borrowing less dividends and loan repayments. Cash rose $50,000.

scenes.heading: Free cash flow
scenes.say: Free cash flow is cash from operations less capital expenditures and dividends: just $20,000. Bluestem has little cash left for new projects without borrowing.
Here we're reading the statement. Building it from scratch is a big topic in Intermediate Accounting Two.

scenes.q: Paying dividends is a cash outflow from:
scenes.say: Quick check. Paying dividends is a cash outflow from which activity? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Notes and disclosure
videos.take: Notes explain policies, contingencies, commitments and subsequent events; they're part of the statements

scenes.say: The numbers are only half of Bluestem's annual report. The notes often matter more.

scenes.heading: Common notes
scenes.say: Common notes include the summary of significant accounting policies, like Bluestem's inventory method and depreciation lives; contingencies, like lawsuits; commitments and debt terms; and events after the balance sheet date.

Subsequent events happen after the balance sheet date but before the statements are issued. If they give evidence about conditions at year-end, like a customer's bankruptcy that confirms a bad receivable, adjust the numbers. If they're new conditions, like a fire in February, disclose them.

scenes.heading: Disclosure techniques
scenes.say: Information can be disclosed through parenthetical explanations on the face of the statements, notes, cross-references and contra accounts, and supporting schedules.
Disclosure is not a substitute for proper recognition. If an item meets the recognition criteria, a note explaining it doesn't make the omission acceptable.

scenes.q: In February, a fire destroys Bluestem's warehouse before the statements are issued. Treatment?
scenes.say: Quick check. In February, a fire destroys Bluestem's warehouse before the statements are issued. Treatment? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B: disclose it. The fire is a new condition after year-end.

warmup: Bluestem has $4 million of assets on its balance sheet. Would you pay $4 million for the company? Why or why not?
Book vs market value; omitted intangibles; historical cost.
acts: Explain liquidity, solvency and financial flexibility, and name one balance sheet item that bears on each.
Liquidity: cash, receivables. Solvency: long-term debt vs assets. Flexibility: unused credit, low leverage.
Classify: prepaid insurance (12 months); land held for speculation; patents; bond sinking fund; inventory; equipment.
Current; long-term investment; intangible; long-term investment (restricted); current; PP&E.
Classify: accounts payable; current portion of mortgage; unearned revenue; bonds due in 8 years; dividends declared; treasury stock.
Current; current; current; long-term; current; contra equity.

Compute the current, quick and debt-to-assets ratios for a company with cash $50,000, receivables $150,000, inventory $300,000, current liabilities $250,000, total liabilities $600,000, total assets $1,500,000.
Classify each cash flow: interest paid; sale of old truck; issuing common stock; purchase of equipment; collections from customers; repayment of loan principal.
Operating; investing; financing; investing; operating; financing.

Decide whether to adjust or disclose: (a) customer with a December receivable declares bankruptcy in January; (b) Bluestem issues bonds in February; (c) lawsuit from a November accident settled in January.
(a) Adjust; (b) disclose; (c) adjust (condition existed at year-end).
case: Bluestem's loan requires a current ratio of at least 2.0. On December 31, current assets are $1,400,000 and current liabilities $650,000. The founder suggests (1) using $150,000 of cash to pay down accounts payable on December 30; (2) reclassifying $200,000 of inventory as a long-term asset; (3) delaying a large aluminum purchase on account from December 29 to January 3.
Compute the current ratio after idea 1.

Idea 1: 1,250,000 ÷ 500,000 = 2.5 (legitimate; it raises the ratio when it's above 1). Idea 2: not acceptable; inventory held for sale is current. Idea 3: a genuine change in purchase timing is legal but window dressing; if goods arrived in December they must be recorded. Ethical issues: misleading the lender; disclosure of window dressing.
exam: Explain how current assets and current liabilities are defined, and give three examples of each.
One year or operating cycle, whichever longer; cash/receivables/inventory/prepaids; payables/accrued/unearned/current portion of LTD.
Using Bluestem's numbers (CFO $520,000, capex $380,000, dividends $120,000, current assets $1.4m, current liabilities $650,000), compute free cash flow and the current ratio and comment.
FCF $20,000; current ratio 2.15; adequate liquidity but limited discretionary cash; inventory-heavy.

Classify cash flows and compute free cash flow
Apply disclosure requirements, including subsequent events
take: Current = one year or operating cycle
Current portion of debt is current
Notes are part of the statements
